newsitem.title: USA: Unconventional plan for Boston's convention center.
newsitem.headline: Unconventional plan for Boston's convention center.

text.p: Massachusetts Gov. William Weld on Monday proposed a 2.3 percent tax on hotels in Boston and Cambridge to provide the revenue stream for a $700 million convention center.

Weld, testifying before the State Administration Committee, said the proposed convention center would open in 2002, create 18,000 and 4,000 indirect jobs. He also said the new convention center would create a need for an estimated 3,000 new hotel rooms.
"Hyatt is moving ahead with plans to build a new hotel three blocks from the proposed site of the convention center," Weld told the committee, adding that Loews Corp "is also scouting locations."
Every 1,000 room hotel would generate 6,000 permanent jobs, Weld said.
His proposal requires the hotel tax be approved by voters in Boston and Cambridge.

Under the governor's plan, Boston will put up at least $125 million for the "acquisition, relocation, demolition and remediation costs," while the state will use the revenues from the proposed hotel tax to finance a $575 million bond issue.

Weld told reporters after he thought the "few remaining differences on financing can be bridged...I'm hopeful that one way or another this baby's going to get delivered before the Legislature breaks" for recess in July.
But Boston Mayor Thomas Menino was no so certain the referendum aspect would survive the Legislature and Weld said if it was not included, he would veto the bill.
"There's no way the voters of Boston are going to approve a tax," Menino said, suggesting that having voters decide was not a good way to conduct tax policy.
Meanwhile, a study conducted for the Pioneer Institute for Public Policy Research and released last month found the need for a new convention center in Boston may not really exist.

"The proposal for a new Boston convention center stands an an obvious case of goal confusion. If the intent of Boston and the Commonwealth is to build a massaive box, that can certainly be accomplished," said the report's author, Heywood Sanders, of the Department of Urban Administration at Trinity University in San Antonio, Texas.

"Yet if the intent of the public investment is to boost Boston's hospitality industry and its job generation, the experience of both the Hynes (Convention Center in Boston) and other cities suggests that the causal link may well be reversed...New hotels in Boston are likely to require a substantial commitment of public resources beyond the development of the city," the report notes.

It points to Philadelphia, which is employing a host of public subsidy vehicles in its search for rooms. One development, a proposed new $105 million Loews hotel, will receive more than $38 million in public financing.
